passages.happening:
It is just before the Passover. Jesus knows that his hour has come to leave this world and go to the Father. John says, “Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end” (verse 1).

They are at supper. The devil has already put it into the heart of Judas to betray Jesus (verse 2). Jesus knows that the Father has put all things into his hands, and that he came from God and is going back to God (verse 3). So he gets up from the table. He takes off his outer clothes and ties a towel around his waist. He pours water into a basin and begins to wash his disciples' feet, drying them with the towel (verses 4-5).

He comes to Peter. “Lord, are You going to wash my feet?” (verse 6). Jesus says Peter will understand later. “Never shall You wash my feet!” says Peter. Jesus answers, “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me” (verse 8). Then Peter swings the other way: “not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!” (verse 9).

Jesus tells him that a person who has bathed needs only to wash his feet. “And you are clean, though not all of you” (verse 10). He said this because he knew who would betray him (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
People walked dusty roads in sandals. So when guests arrived, water was brought for their feet. Often the guests washed their own feet. When someone else did it, it was usually a slave or a servant of low rank. Abigail shows how lowly the job was when she says to David's men, “Here is your maidservant, ready to serve and to wash the feet of my lord’s servants” (1 Samuel 25:41). Normally the lower person washed the feet of the higher, not the other way round.

So picture the room. The disciples are lying on couches around the table, feet stretched out behind them. Their teacher gets up, strips down to a towel like a slave at work, and goes from one pair of dirty feet to the next. No wonder Peter protests. In his world, a teacher would not normally do this for his pupils.

Notice who is in the circle. Jesus knows Judas will betray him (verse 11). He washes Judas's feet too.

John says this meal was ‘just before the Passover’. In Matthew, Mark and Luke the Last Supper is the Passover meal. Christians explain the difference in several ways: some think John reckoned the feast differently, some think the groups in Jerusalem used different calendars, some think one account is shaped to show Jesus as the Passover lamb. The question is open. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, washing was part of coming near to God. The priests had to wash “their hands and feet” before serving at the altar (Exodus 30:19). David prays, ‘wash me, and I will be whiter than snow’ (Psalm 51:7).

Hospitality began with water for the feet. When three visitors came to Abraham, he said, “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree” (Genesis 18:4).
passages.hard:
Is foot washing a rite Christians should keep? Jesus says, ‘you also should wash one another’s feet’ (verse 14). Churches have answered differently, and each has its reasons.

Some churches keep foot washing as an ordinance, a practice Christ commanded for his church, often joined to the Lord's Supper. Among them are the Church of the Brethren, many Mennonite churches, Seventh-day Adventists, and Free Will Baptists. They point to the plain words, ‘you also should wash’ and ‘I have set you an example’. The Catholic Church and some other churches wash feet at the service on the Thursday before Easter, often called Maundy Thursday; in the Catholic rite it may be done, but is not required. Many churches do not wash feet at all. They read the command as a call to humble service of every kind, of which washing feet was the everyday example in Jesus' world. These notes take no side. All agree that the heart of the command is to serve one another in love.

And what does ‘you have no part with Me’ mean? Jesus is saying more than ‘let me wash your feet’. Peter must let Jesus serve him, and in the end cleanse him, through his death. Many Christians hear in ‘whoever has already bathed’ a picture of the cleansing that comes once, when we first come to Christ, and the daily washing that we still need.
passages.asks: Peter found it harder to be served than to serve. Many people do. Ask whether you can let Jesus do for you what you cannot do for yourself. And notice that Jesus knew everything, where he came from and where he was going, and what he did with that knowledge was pick up a towel. Ask what you do with the power and the knowledge you have.

passages.t: I have set you an example
passages.happening:
When he has finished, Jesus puts his outer clothes back on and returns to his place. “Do you know what I have done for you?” he asks (verse 12). “You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am. So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet” (verses 13-14).

“I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you” (verse 15). No servant is greater than his master. No messenger is greater than the one who sent him. “If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them” (verse 17).

Then Jesus says he is not speaking of all of them. Scripture must be fulfilled: “The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me” (verse 18). He tells them now, so that when it happens they will believe that he is the one he says he is (verse 19). And whoever receives the one Jesus sends receives Jesus, and whoever receives Jesus receives the Father who sent him (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord’ were titles a disciple would use for his rabbi and master. Jesus does not deny them. He says they are right. That is what makes the foot washing so striking. He does not stop being Lord to serve. He serves as Lord.

To share bread at a table made a bond of loyalty in that world. To betray someone you had eaten with was a special kind of treachery.

‘Lifted up his heel’ pictures a sudden kick, or tripping someone up. Some readers think it may also picture showing someone the sole of your foot, which is still an insult in much of the Middle East today. Either way, it means turning on a friend.

‘That I am He’ (verse 19) is, in Greek, the same ‘I am’ Jesus used in chapter 8 (8:24, 8:28, 8:58).
passages.ot: The quotation is from Psalm 41, a psalm of David: “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9). Another psalm feels the same wound: “For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure” (Psalm 55:12). The king of Israel was betrayed by a friend, and so is Jesus.
passages.hard: Does ‘no servant is greater than his master’ mean people should put up with mistreatment? No. Jesus' example is love freely given by the one with power. It is not a command to stay under someone who abuses you. Jesus served his friends; he did not hand himself over to be used by them. If you are being hurt by someone, in a home, a workplace or a church, humble service does not mean silence. Seeking safety and help is not disobedience. Elsewhere Jesus asks a guard who struck him, ‘why did you strike Me?’ (18:23).
passages.asks: ‘If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.’ Knowing that Jesus served is not enough. Ask whose feet you could wash this week: what lowly, unseen, unthanked task you could do for someone, without being asked. And notice that Jesus served the man who would betray him. Ask whether there is someone you serve only if they deserve it.

passages.t: One of you will betray Me
passages.happening:
Jesus becomes “troubled in spirit” and says plainly, “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will betray Me” (verse 21). The disciples look at one another, not knowing whom he means (verse 22).

One of them, “the one whom Jesus loved”, is reclining next to him (verse 23). Peter signals to him to ask who it is. Leaning back against Jesus, he asks, “Lord, who is it?” (verse 25).

Jesus answers, “It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it.” He dips the bread and gives it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot (verse 26). “And when Judas had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him” (verse 27). Jesus says to him, “What you are about to do, do quickly.”

No one at the table understands. Judas keeps the money bag, so some think Jesus has sent him to buy food for the feast, or to give something to the poor (verses 28-29). As soon as Judas has taken the bread, he goes out. John says, “Judas went out into the night” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Here, for the first time, John speaks of ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’. He never gives his name. He appears again at the cross (19:26-27), at the empty tomb (20:2-10), and by the lake (21:7, 21:20), and the book's last chapter says he is the witness behind it (21:24). From the late second century the church said he was John, the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Others think he was a follower from Jerusalem who was not one of the Twelve, perhaps the man called John the elder. The book page sets out the views. Nearly all agree on one thing: the book rests on the memory of someone who was there.

At a meal like this the guests lay on couches, each leaning on his left elbow. So the disciple next to Jesus could lean back against his chest and ask a quiet question. Peter, further away, had to signal across the table.

The morsel was a piece of bread dipped in a shared dish. Judas was close enough to take it from Jesus' own hand. Many readers think that a host giving a guest such a piece was a mark of friendship. Whether or not that was a custom, Jesus offers it to the man he knows will betray him.

‘Into the night’ is more than the time of day. All through John, light and darkness stand for faith and unbelief. Judas walks out of the light and into the dark.
passages.ot: The Old Testament knows the pain of betrayal by someone close. David's trusted adviser Ahithophel turned against him and joined his son Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15:31). The psalm Jesus quoted says, “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9).
passages.hard:
If Satan entered Judas, and Scripture had foretold the betrayal, was Judas to blame? Christians have answered carefully. John himself shows that Judas had his own motive: he stole from the money bag (12:6). Jesus washed his feet and handed him the bread, which many readers take as a last offer of friendship. Many readers note that Satan entered a man who had already let greed in. Luke also says, “Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot” (Luke 22:3). Christians who stress God's purpose and those who stress human choice explain differently how God's foreknowledge and Judas's act fit together. They agree that the betrayal was truly Judas's act, and that God was not taken by surprise.

What happened to Judas in the end? Matthew tells of his remorse and death (Matthew 27:3-5), and the note there speaks of it with care. These notes do not say what God did with Judas. That belongs to God.

Notice too what the other disciples did. When Jesus said ‘one of you’, they did not point at Judas. Each wondered about himself (verse 22). John does not let any reader stand outside the circle.
passages.asks: Being betrayed by someone close is one of the deepest wounds there is. Jesus felt it: he was ‘troubled in spirit’. If someone you trusted has betrayed you, being shaken by it is not a lack of faith. Jesus was shaken too. Ask where you can take that wound. And ask, as the disciples did, whether there is a door in your own heart you have left open to the dark.

passages.happening:
When Judas has gone out, Jesus says, “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him” (verse 31). God will glorify the Son, and will do it at once (verse 32).

Then he speaks to them tenderly. “Little children, I am with you only a little while longer.” They will look for him, but where he is going, they cannot come (verse 33).

“A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another” (verses 34-35).
passages.hearers:
It is a strange moment to speak of glory. Judas has just gone out to betray him. But in John, Jesus' glory is seen most clearly at the cross. The moment the betrayal begins, the hour of glory begins.

‘Little children’ is how a father speaks to his family at a farewell. Later, the First Letter of John uses the same words for its readers again and again.

The Thursday before Easter is called Maundy Thursday in English. Most scholars think ‘Maundy’ comes from the Latin word mandatum, ‘commandment’, the first word of verse 34 in the old Latin Bible: ‘a new commandment I give you’. Those words were sung during the foot washing on that day.
passages.ot: Love one another was not new in itself. The law of Moses said, “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), and it said the same of the foreigner living among Israel (Leviticus 19:34). What is new is the measure: ‘As I have loved you’. The love of the one who just washed their feet, and who will lay down his life, is now the pattern.
passages.hard:
If the commandment is ‘new’, was there no love before? There was. Leviticus already commanded it. Christians explain the newness in a few ways. The pattern is new: Jesus' own self-giving love, washing feet and going to the cross. The community is new: a family made by Jesus, from every kind of person. And the time is new: the age God promised has begun. The First Letter of John says the commandment is both old and new (1 John 2:7-8).

Does ‘one another’ mean Christians should love only other Christians? No. Jesus also told his followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44) and to love their neighbor, and he showed that a neighbor can be anyone (Luke 10:29-37). Here he speaks of love inside his own circle, which the world will see. A church that loves outsiders but cannot love its own members is not keeping this command. Neither is one that loves only its own.
passages.asks: Jesus did not say people would know his disciples by their doctrine, their success or their morals, important as those are. He said they would know them by their love for one another. Ask what an outsider would see if they watched your church for a year. And ask whom in your own church you find hardest to love as Jesus loved you.

passages.happening:
Peter asks, “Lord, where are You going?” Jesus answers, “Where I am going, you cannot follow Me now, but you will follow later” (verse 36).

Peter will not accept it. “Lord,” he says, “why can’t I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You” (verse 37).

Jesus answers him with a question: “Will you lay down your life for Me?” Then he says, “Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Peter means every word. He is the one who will draw a sword in the garden to defend Jesus (18:10). His courage is real. What he does not know is how weak he is.

Roosters crow in the last hours of the night, before dawn. Mark's account says ‘before the rooster crows twice’ (Mark 14:30). The point is the same: before this night is over.

‘You will follow later’ is a promise, not only a warning. At the end of the book the risen Jesus will restore Peter, and tell him that he will one day give his life, and then say to him, ‘Follow Me’ (21:18-19).
passages.ot: Even the bravest in Scripture failed. Elijah, after his great victory on Mount Carmel, ran for his life in fear, sat under a broom tree, and asked to die (1 Kings 19:3-4). God did not throw him away. An angel woke him and fed him, and God later sent him back to his work (1 Kings 19:5-8, 15). The Psalms are full of people who failed and were restored: “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).
passages.hard:
Why tell Peter in advance that he will fail? Not to shame him. Luke records that Jesus said, “But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Jesus knew Peter would fall, and he had already prayed for his return.

If you have failed Jesus, perhaps badly, perhaps more than once, notice this. Jesus knew about Peter's denial before it happened, and he did not send Peter away. He kept him at the table. After the denial Peter ‘wept bitterly’ (Matthew 26:75), and in John the risen Jesus met him by the lake and asked him three times, ‘do you love Me?’ (21:15-17). Three denials, three chances to say yes. Failure is not the end of the story for anyone who comes back.
passages.asks: Peter's promise was sincere, and he still failed. Ask where you are counting on your own courage. And if you are carrying the memory of a time you denied Jesus, by your words, your silence or your life, notice that Jesus told Peter ‘you will follow later’ before he ever failed. The way back was open before he fell.
